priorityqueue-min-heap.title: Dequeue by priority with PriorityQueue
priorityqueue-min-heap.short: Efficiently remove elements in ascending priority order.
priorityqueue-min-heap.summary: PriorityQueue<TElement,TPriority> associates each element with a priority and dequeues the element with the lowest priority first. It is useful for path finding, schedulers, and other ordered work.
priorityqueue-min-heap.why: Sorting an entire list whenever work is added maintains more ordering than is needed. PriorityQueue maintains the ordering required for enqueue and dequeue operations.
priorityqueue-min-heap.tips: Insertion order is not guaranteed among elements with equal priorities. To model highest-value-first behavior, transform the priority or provide a suitable comparer.

immutablearray-snapshot.title: Represent immutable snapshots with ImmutableArray
immutablearray-snapshot.short: Create a new array state without modifying the original value.
immutablearray-snapshot.summary: ImmutableArray<T> represents an array whose contents cannot be changed in place. Operations such as Add return a new ImmutableArray while the original remains unchanged.
immutablearray-snapshot.why: When shared data must not be changed later, immutability can be represented by the type rather than only by a convention between callers.
immutablearray-snapshot.tips: The objects stored inside the array can still be mutable. For many edits at once, consider using an ImmutableArray builder before producing the final snapshot.

random-shared-concurrent.title: Use Random.Shared for shared random generation
random-shared-concurrent.short: Use the shared Random instance safely from concurrent code.
random-shared-concurrent.summary: Random.Shared provides a shared Random instance that can be used from multiple threads. It avoids creating a new generator for every simple random operation.
random-shared-concurrent.why: For ordinary random values, Random.Shared avoids both repeated construction and the need to add your own locking around one shared Random instance.
random-shared-concurrent.tips: Random is not cryptographically secure; use RandomNumberGenerator for security-sensitive values. Tests that require reproducible sequences are better served by a Random with a fixed seed.

argumentnullexception-throwifnull.title: Validate null arguments with ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull
argumentnullexception-throwifnull.short: Reject a required null argument at the method boundary.
argumentnullexception-throwifnull.summary: ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull throws ArgumentNullException when a required argument is null. It provides a compact way to state a method precondition at its entry point.
argumentnullexception-throwifnull.why: Allowing null to flow deeper until a NullReferenceException occurs makes it harder to identify which caller violated the API contract.
argumentnullexception-throwifnull.tips: Do not use it when null is a valid input. Public APIs can combine nullable annotations with runtime validation according to their contract.

task-waitasync-timeout.title: Add a timeout to a Task wait with WaitAsync
task-waitasync-timeout.short: Wait for an existing Task with a timeout or cancellation token.
task-waitasync-timeout.summary: Task.WaitAsync lets a caller wait for a Task with a timeout or CancellationToken without changing the Task itself. A timeout causes TimeoutException.
task-waitasync-timeout.why: It expresses a bounded wait directly instead of rebuilding the pattern with Task.Delay and Task.WhenAny. The wait ending and the underlying operation ending are separate events.
task-waitasync-timeout.tips: A WaitAsync timeout does not automatically stop the original Task. If the operation itself must stop, design it to accept and observe a CancellationToken.

string-create-formatting.title: Build culture-specific strings with string.Create
string-create-formatting.short: Specify formatting culture while creating an interpolated string.
string-create-formatting.summary: An interpolated-string overload of string.Create can explicitly select the IFormatProvider used to format values. This is useful for stable machine-readable representations.
string-create-formatting.why: Decimal separators, dates, and other formatted values can vary with the current culture. Storage and interchange formats sometimes require output independent of the display environment.
string-create-formatting.tips: User-facing text should normally respect the user's culture. Use InvariantCulture where a stable machine-oriented representation is intentionally required.

record-with-expression.title: Copy and change records with a with expression
record-with-expression.short: Create a new record while changing only selected members.
record-with-expression.summary: A with expression creates a new record based on an existing one and changes the specified members. It is useful for expressing configuration and state updates as values.
record-with-expression.why: When the original value should remain available, a with expression makes the changed fields clearer than manually copying every property.
record-with-expression.tips: A with expression is not a deep clone of referenced objects. Mutable objects stored in members can still be shared between the old and new records.

async-lock-semaphoreslim.title: Use SemaphoreSlim for asynchronous mutual exclusion
async-lock-semaphoreslim.short: Do not put await inside lock; use an asynchronously waitable gate.
async-lock-semaphoreslim.summary: A normal lock statement cannot contain await. When asynchronous work must run one operation at a time, SemaphoreSlim.WaitAsync can acquire a gate and Release can return it in a finally block.
async-lock-semaphoreslim.why: Synchronous locking and asynchronous waiting have different execution models. Converting asynchronous work into blocking waits can cause stalls or deadlocks.
async-lock-semaphoreslim.tips: Release in a finally block. When WaitAsync accepts a CancellationToken, structure the code so Release happens only after the wait successfully acquired the semaphore.

linq-any-before-enumeration.title: Use Any() instead of Count() > 0 for existence checks
linq-any-before-enumeration.short: Use Any when the question is only whether a sequence contains an element.
linq-any-before-enumeration.summary: For IEnumerable<T>, Any() directly expresses an existence check. Count() can require traversing the complete sequence when a cheap count is not available.
linq-any-before-enumeration.why: If only the presence of one element matters, evaluation can stop as soon as the first element is found instead of counting every element.
linq-any-before-enumeration.tips: Arrays and List<T> expose cheap Length or Count properties that are also clear. Be careful not to repeatedly evaluate lazy sequences with side effects.

stream-position-after-read.title: Check Stream position before reusing a stream
stream-position-after-read.short: Remember that reading usually advances a Stream toward its end.
stream-position-after-read.summary: Reading a Stream normally advances its Position. If another consumer must read the same seekable Stream from the beginning, reset its position before handing it over.
stream-position-after-read.why: Passing a Stream immediately after reading it to the end can make the next consumer observe an empty input even though the underlying data still exists.
stream-position-after-read.tips: Not every Stream supports seeking. Check CanSeek; for non-seekable streams, design the pipeline so the data is consumed once or buffered deliberately when necessary.
